emails.subject: Account 88-4417 — estimated readings since March
emails.body:
Dear Northlight,

My account has been billed on estimates since March. The November bill is $612 against a monthly average of $190 last winter, and the estimate assumes consumption I could not physically have used — I was away for seven weeks of that period and the house was empty.

I submitted my own reading on 14 October through your website. The November bill does not use it. I have the confirmation number.

I want to separate two things.

The first is the money, and I expect that to resolve itself once an actual reading is used. I am not worried about it and I am not asking for a gesture.

The second is why I am on estimates at all. Your meter reader has attended four times this year according to your own bill, and each visit is recorded as "no access". My meter is in an unlocked outdoor cupboard on the front wall of the house, visible from the street, with no gate. I do not understand what access was unavailable, and I would like to, because if the visits are being recorded as attempted and are not happening, that is a different problem from a meter that is hard to reach.

I would rather ask than assume.

Sincerely,
Ingeborg Halvorsen

emails.subject: RE: Account 88-4417 — estimated readings since March
emails.body:
Dear Ms Halvorsen,

On the money: your 14 October reading was submitted correctly and was not applied because it fell outside the billing window by two days, and our system discards rather than holds a reading in that position. That is a design fault and I have logged it as one. Your bill has been recalculated on your reading and the corrected amount is $214. The difference of $398 has been credited today.

On the second question, which you were right to ask separately.

The four visits were made and the "no access" code was applied incorrectly. Our readers use a handheld device where "no access" is the default code and requires no reason to be entered, while every other outcome requires a note. When a reader cannot complete a visit for any reason — running late, a dog barking two doors down, a device fault — "no access" is the path of least resistance and it is indistinguishable afterwards from a genuinely inaccessible meter.

I cannot tell you which of those applied on your four visits, because the system did not capture it. That is the honest answer and I know it is unsatisfying.

What changes: from next month "no access" requires a reason code and a photograph. That was already scheduled for the spring; I have asked for it to be brought forward, and I will tell you plainly that I do not yet know whether that request will be granted.

Your meter is now flagged for a physical read in December regardless of the route schedule.

Regards,
Augustin Moreau
Billing Resolutions

passages.title: Why Insulation Saves Less Than the Estimate Says
passages.content:
Home energy retrofits are promoted with figures that are calculated honestly and are, in practice, usually wrong. Measured savings after insulation are consistently lower than modelled savings, and the gap is large enough that it deserves an explanation rather than an accusation.

The most-discussed reason is the rebound effect, sometimes called comfort taking. A household that could not afford to heat its home adequately does not, after insulation, keep the same temperature and pocket the money. It heats more rooms, for longer, to a temperature it previously could not reach. The energy saving is smaller than modelled because part of the benefit was taken as warmth rather than as cash — which is not a failure of the policy unless the policy was only ever about carbon, and it is frequently sold as being about bills.

Less discussed and more consequential is that models assume installation quality. A cavity wall filled unevenly, insulation compressed during fitting, or a gap left where a pipe passes through a wall can remove a substantial share of the theoretical benefit, and none of it is visible once the work is finished. Verification is the weakest link in most retrofit programmes, and the incentive structure rarely helps: installers are typically paid on completion rather than on measured performance.

Occupancy assumptions are a third source of divergence. Models generally assume a standard heating pattern and a standard household. A house occupied all day by someone at home, or a household that has always heated one room, diverges from that assumption in opposite directions and by large amounts. The modelled figure describes an average household that few actual households resemble.

There is also a sequencing problem that generates real disappointment. Insulating a house without addressing ventilation can raise humidity and produce condensation and mould, which is both a health issue and the most common reason households report regretting the work. Doing the measures in the wrong order can leave a home warmer, cheaper to heat and unpleasant to live in.

The reasonable conclusion is not that insulation does not work; it reliably does, and the measured savings are real even where they are smaller than promised. It is that programmes should quote ranges rather than point estimates, fund verification as seriously as installation, and stop describing comfort taken as a benefit as though it were a shortfall.

passages.title: Who Should Pay to Insulate Rented Homes?

viewpoints.name: Minister Rosalind Okonjo
viewpoints.text: We placed the obligation on landlords and I would defend that, while conceding the objection that it is a cost imposed on one party for a benefit received by another. That is true and it is not unusual — building standards work the same way. What makes this case different, and what I did not anticipate, is how many small landlords own a single property and cannot finance the work at any interest rate they can obtain. The policy assumed a landlord who is a business. Many are a pension.

viewpoints.name: Declan Whitfield, landlord
viewpoints.text: I own two flats and I will comply, so read this as a complaint about sequencing rather than principle. The standard was announced with a deadline and no finance mechanism for eighteen months, so everyone waited, and now the entire sector is bidding for the same installers in the same window. Prices have risen accordingly. Announce the funding and the requirement together and the same work costs less and gets done sooner — the delay between the two is itself a cost, and tenants pay part of it.

viewpoints.name: Aisling Ferrero, tenant
viewpoints.text: My flat was insulated last year and my bills went up. The work raised the temperature the heating could reach, so the system now runs to a thermostat setting it never used to achieve, and nobody explained that would happen. I am warmer and I am poorer, and I would still choose warm — but I was told bills would fall, and when they did not I had no way to tell whether the work was faulty or whether I had been told something untrue. Give tenants a way to check.

viewpoints.name: Dr Konstantin Weber, building physicist
viewpoints.text: The regulatory standard measures the fabric of the building and says almost nothing about how it performs occupied. Two identical flats with identical certificates can differ by a wide margin in real consumption, depending on ventilation, orientation, the neighbours' heating and how the controls are set. I support the requirement. I would simply note that we are regulating a proxy, and that a certificate improving does not reliably mean a household's bill falls — which is precisely the promise being made.
